design_detail: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42017059224) with random-effects meta-analysis of the association between smoked cannabis (called marijuana in the paper) and respiratory symptoms (cough, sputum production, wheezing, dyspnea), obstructive lung disease and pulmonary function, in people older than 12 years with at least 30 days of lifetime use. Five databases were searched from 1 January 1973 to 30 April 2018. 22 studies were included (10 prospective cohort, 12 cross-sectional); 3 were rated high risk of bias. Prospective and cross-sectional studies were pooled separately and only when at least 2 studies of low or moderate risk of bias had usable data: 5 of 13 outcomes could be pooled. Strength of evidence was graded by the AHRQ method.
can_establish: The average size of the association between cannabis use and cough, sputum production, wheezing, dyspnea and chronic bronchitis in the published English-language studies up to April 2018, split by cohort and cross-sectional designs, and how thin the evidence is for lung-function tests and obstructive lung disease.
cannot_establish: Causation or the effect of cannabis apart from tobacco (the main text does not say whether the pooled ratios were adjusted, and several studies reported people who smoked both together); effects of heavy long-term use on lung function (few people had more than 20 joint-years and cohorts were young); dose-response; differences between smoking, vaping and eating cannabis (only smoking is described); and whether the published literature is affected by publication bias (not assessed).

sample.recruitment: PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library, 1 January 1973 (the year Oregon decriminalised possession) to 30 April 2018, plus author and reference tracking. English-language observational (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) and interventional studies in people older than 12 years with at least 30 days of lifetime cannabis use; studies reporting only short-term laboratory outcomes and studies with fewer than 10 people who used cannabis were excluded. 1265 abstracts were identified, 927 selected for further evaluation, 70 read in full and 3 added by reference tracking: 73 candidate articles, 22 included (Results › Literature Search; Methods).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As above. The 30-day lifetime cut-off was chosen by the authors to ensure meaningful exposure. Route of use is not a stated inclusion criterion, but every exposure described in the text is smoking (joints, joint-years).
sample.demographics: Study-level tables are in the Supplement (a PDF, not opened). The text names the largest cohorts: CARDIA (5115 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start, followed 20 years), the Dunedin birth cohort (1037 children born in 1972 and 1973; mean follow-up 15 years for symptoms, 10 years from age 18 to 32 for lung function), a random sample of the population of Tucson, Arizona (n = 1802, surveyed 1981 to 1988), a Los Angeles cohort (299 people at the start, mean 3.0 joints a day for 9.8 years) and SPIROMICS (1174 people currently or formerly smoking tobacco). The authors state that cohorts were young overall and cannabis exposure limited.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. The one Los Angeles cohort that contributed to the pooled prospective symptom estimates and to the chronic-bronchitis result lost 49% of participants to follow-up.
sample.selection_effects: English language only; no registry, grey-literature or expert search described in the main text; the cut-off of 30 lifetime days and a lower limit of 10 people who used cannabis. The pooled prospective symptom estimates rest on two cohorts with very different exposure (about once a week for a year in Dunedin; about 3 joints a day for 9.8 years in Los Angeles). Two low-risk cross-sectional studies of symptoms (refs 26 and 27) are not among the 4 pooled; the text does not say why. Studies in people who smoke tobacco only (SPIROMICS) or with cannabis and tobacco smoking combined (NHANES, SPIROMICS) are hard to read as effects of cannabis alone. Heavy long-term exposure is thin: across all prospective lung-function evaluations only 243 people (131 cannabis-only) had more than 20 joint-years (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used: self-reported cannabis use, quantified in different ways (monthly, weekly or daily use; joint-years; cigarette-years). The authors say this varied exposure measurement is a main source of heterogeneity. No biological verification is described in the main text.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Across all outcomes and studies, 1255 participants had more than 10 joint-years of exposure and 756 people who smoked cannabis only had more than 20 joint-years (Results › Study Characteristics); across all prospective lung-function evaluations only 243 people (131 cannabis-only) had more than 20 joint-years (Discussion, 4th paragraph). The authors note that 1 joint a day for 20 years is 7300 joints. Route: smoking, as described; vaping and eating are not covered.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco is the key confounder. The authors rated a study low risk of bias only if tobacco use was assessed and adjusted for and people who smoked cannabis only could be told apart from people who smoked both. The symptom comparisons were of people who used cannabis against people who used neither cannabis nor tobacco (Methods › Data Synthesis and Analysis, 1st paragraph); whether the cannabis group in each pooled study included people who also smoked tobacco is not described in the main text. NHANES and SPIROMICS reported lung-function results for combined cannabis and tobacco smoking only.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the two pooled prospective studies each reported that stopping cannabis was followed by fewer respiratory symptoms (Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: People who did not use cannabis (for the symptom comparisons, people who used neither cannabis nor tobacco), as defined in each primary study.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. The main text does not say whether the pooled ratios were adjusted; the methods say ratios were extracted when reported and calculated from counts otherwise (so some are probably crude).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed by the review. Cross-sectional studies (12 of 22) cannot separate pre-existing differences in airways from effects of smoking. CARDIA and Dunedin enrolled people when young, before most of their cannabis exposure.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparators were meant to be people who did not smoke tobacco for the symptom pools; other drug and alcohol use are not discussed.

outcomes.instruments: Self-reported cough, sputum production, wheezing and dyspnea (definitions vary: the authors give 'most days for 3 consecutive months' against 'more than 6 times a day' for cough); chronic bronchitis and COPD; spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1-FVC ratio); airway resistance and specific conductance of airways; other respiratory outcomes (outpatient visits, hospital admission, airway reactivity to methacholine).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not appraised by the review beyond the risk-of-bias ratings. The authors state that tobacco-related FEV1 loss becomes measurable only after about 5 to 10 pack-years (36,500 to 73,000 cigarettes), and that exposure in the included cannabis studies may be too low to show a comparable change.
outcomes.operationalization: Respiratory symptoms were pooled as risk ratios (and risk differences) of cough, sputum production, wheezing and dyspnea; lung function was kept as mean differences and narrative synthesis because most studies reported 1 or 2 indices.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 13 distinct outcomes were identified (Supplement Figure 1); 5 were pooled.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers screened all titles, abstracts and full texts independently (Cohen kappa 0.81 on 80 random abstracts); four reviewers extracted data and rated risk of bias independently; three reviewers graded the strength of evidence together.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects model (Paule-Mandel tau-squared, Knapp-Hartung small-sample adjustment, R package meta 3.3.3); numbers of participants in the pooled analyses are not given in the main text. Prospective cohorts, 2 studies (Dunedin and Los Angeles), people who used cannabis against people who did not: cough RR 2.04 (95% CI 1.02 to 4.06), risk difference 0.07 (0.02 to 0.13); sputum production RR 3.84 (1.62 to 9.07), RD 0.12 (-0.02 to 0.25); low heterogeneity; after the Knapp-Hartung small-sample adjustment the pooled RRs were not significant (cough P = 0.10; sputum P = 0.20; Figure 2 legend). Cross-sectional studies, 4 pooled (1 low and 3 moderate risk of bias): cough RR 4.37 (1.71 to 11.19), RD 0.18 (0.15 to 0.21); sputum RR 3.40 (1.99 to 5.79), RD 0.14 (0.10 to 0.17); wheezing RR 2.83 (1.89 to 4.23), RD 0.22 (0.14 to 0.29); dyspnea RR 1.56 (1.33 to 1.83), RD 0.06 (-0.01 to 0.13); chronic bronchitis (3 studies) RR 2.28 (0.68 to 7.72), RD 0.06 (-0.04 to 0.16); Knapp-Hartung P: cough 0.05, sputum 0.05, wheezing 0.01, dyspnea below 0.01, chronic bronchitis 0.31 (Figure 3 legend). Lung function was not pooled; single-study results are in the key findings. I-squared values are in the forest plots (images, not read); the text calls heterogeneity low in the prospective pools and high for wheezing in the cross-sectional pools.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Ratios were extracted or calculated from counts; the text does not say whether adjusted estimates were preferred. Risk-of-bias ratings (Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies) took account of tobacco adjustment.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42017059224. The protocol also covered respiratory tract neoplasms, which this paper says it does not report. The registry record was not read, so differences between record and paper were not compared.
analysis.selective_reporting: Per-study estimates for most lung-function outcomes are in Supplement Tables 2 to 5 (PDF, not opened). The paper states that it reports complete data for all analyses. The paper does not say where the protocol's neoplasm outcomes are reported.
analysis.power: Not formally addressed. The prospective symptom pools contain 2 studies, so their intervals are those of two cohorts rather than a distribution of studies. The authors say the cohorts were young and cannabis exposure limited, which limits the ability to detect lung-function loss.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 22 studies of mostly young people with limited cannabis exposure (the authors' description), smoking cannabis was associated with more cough, sputum production and wheezing against not using cannabis or tobacco, in both cohort and cross-sectional pools (cross-sectional wheezing RR 2.83, cough RR 4.37). In the two prospective studies pooled for cough and sputum the intervals excluded 1, but the Knapp-Hartung adjusted P values were 0.10 and 0.20. Lung-function tests showed no clear fall in FEV1 in the low-risk cohorts at the low exposure they had (CARDIA: -18 mL, CI -42 to 6.1), a higher FVC in several studies, and one cross-sectional signal at more than 20 joint-years (FEV1-FVC ratio below 70%, OR 2.1, CI 1.1 to 3.9). Airway resistance was higher in all 4 studies that measured it. Chronic bronchitis and COPD could not be settled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Conclusion: "Low-strength evidence suggests that smoking marijuana is associated with cough, sputum production, and wheezing." The Discussion says use more than once a week for at least 1 year is associated with these symptoms, and says evidence on lung function and obstructive lung disease is insufficient. Gaps: (1) the pooled prospective ratios are presented in the abstract and Results with confidence intervals that exclude 1, while the figure legend shows the method the paper says it used (Knapp-Hartung) gave non-significant results; (2) the 'more than once a week for at least 1 year' threshold is not derived from any analysis shown (no analysis by frequency or duration of use appears in the text, and the inclusion cut-off was 30 lifetime days); (3) the Introduction states that cannabis smoke may contain particulate matter at 20 times the concentration of tobacco smoke, citing a 1975 book chapter, which the review does not test; (4) the Discussion's remark that lung function may not be among cannabis's most important long-term health outcomes is conjecture. Against this, the strength ratings are modest, 'insufficient' is used honestly for lung function (not 'no effect'), and the limitations name low exposure, young cohorts and non-uniform exposure measurement.

timeline.event: Systematic review of cannabis smoking, lung function and respiratory complications (Tetrault et al., cited as ref 38): found an association with symptoms and called for more lung-function data.
CARDIA 20-year cohort: contributes the FEV1 and FVC results of this review (Pletcher et al.)
Two further reviews (Ribeiro and Ind; Martinasek et al., refs 39 and 40): symptoms associated with cannabis smoking; conflicting lung-function results.

National Academies report (searches to August 2016): the committee graded as 'substantial' the association of long-term cannabis smoking with worse respiratory symptoms and more frequent bronchitis episodes and as 'moderate' the association with higher FVC, and found lung-function evidence otherwise inconclusive (committee's wording)
This review: first review to rate risk of bias, pool where possible and grade the strength of evidence, by the authors' account.
Population-based data-linkage cohort study of cannabis use and respiratory and all-cause illness and death (Ontario)

replication.where_it_stands: The symptom finding (more cough, sputum and wheeze in people who smoke cannabis) is consistent across designs but graded low strength here because few studies are at low risk of bias and tobacco co-use is hard to separate. Whether lung function falls with heavy long-term smoking was not answered: the cohorts were young and their exposure low. Studies in this review overlap with others read for this library (CARDIA is also appraised as pletcher_2012), so they do not count as independent replication.

funding.funder: No project funding (stated twice: Role of the Funding Source and Acknowledgments). Salomeh Keyhani was supported by NHLBI grant R01HL130484-01A1; Deborah Korenstein by a National Cancer Institute Cancer Center Support Grant (P30 CA008748) to Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.
funding.declared_conflicts: Authors disclosed no conflicts of interest (ICMJE forms referenced).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of California San Francisco and the San Francisco VA Medical Center, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, the Wright Center for Graduate Medical Education and the University of Toronto. No cannabis- or tobacco-industry ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: Large prospective cohorts of adults followed into middle and older age, with repeated spirometry, measured lifetime cannabis exposure by route and amount, tobacco use recorded in detail and enough people who smoke cannabis only at heavy exposure (for example more than 20 joint-years); or an individual-participant pooling of the existing cohorts (CARDIA, Dunedin, Tucson, Los Angeles) with standardised exposure and symptom definitions.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (older than 12 years, at least 30 lifetime days), exposure (cannabis use), comparison (non-use) and outcomes (symptoms, obstructive lung disease, pulmonary function) are stated.
PROSPERO CRD42017059224 and a PRISMA statement; the protocol also covered neoplasms; deviations from the protocol are not discussed and the registry record was not read.
Cohort, case-control, cross-sectional and interventional designs are named but the choice is not explained.

Five databases with a stated date range (justified by Oregon's 1973 decriminalisation) and reference tracking, but English only without justification, and no registry, grey-literature or expert search described; the search was completed within a few months of publication.
Two reviewers screened all titles and abstracts independently and the same two reviewed full texts, with a third for disagreements; kappa 0.81 on 80 abstracts.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the main text gives the numbers screened and excluded (Figure 1 is an image) but no list of excluded full texts with reasons; the Supplement PDF was not opened and may contain one.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The text describes the main cohorts, their sizes, exposures and risk-of-bias ratings; full study tables are in the Supplement (not opened).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Newcastle-Ottawa Scale or Cochrane tool by four reviewers independently, with a low-risk definition built on tobacco adjustment, follow-up, exposure detail and quantified use, so confounding and selection were assessed; selective reporting was not.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Provisional: the methods say funding source was extracted, but it is not reported in the main text; the Supplement (not opened) may hold it.

Random-effects pooling by design (Paule-Mandel tau-squared, Knapp-Hartung adjustment) is appropriate, but ratios were extracted or calculated from counts without saying that adjusted estimates were preferred or justifying pooled crude ones, studies with very different exposure were pooled (two prospective studies), and the intervals reported in the abstract and text do not appear to be the Knapp-Hartung ones the figure legends refer to.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Only low and moderate risk-of-bias studies were pooled, but no analysis compares them or tests the pooled estimates for bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The abstract names few low-risk studies, limited exposure, young cohorts and non-uniform exposure measurement as limits; strength of evidence is graded and the table comments give reasons.

Heterogeneity is described (low in the prospective pools, high for wheezing) and attributed to non-uniform exposure and outcome definitions, but it was not investigated by subgroup or meta-regression.
Not mentioned in the main text; pools of 2 to 4 studies.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No project funding and no conflicts, with personal grant support named.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence when more than one critical item fails; here items 4 (English only, no registry or grey search), 11 (crude or mixed ratios pooled, intervals not the stated adjusted ones) and 15 (publication bias not examined) fail, item 7 could not be judged without the Supplement, and items 2 and 9 are only partly met. This is a judgment about how far the pooled ratios can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not about the review's value: it is registered, searched five databases, screened and extracted in duplicate, rated risk of bias, graded the evidence cautiously and called lung-function evidence insufficient. The pooled prospective ratios rest on two cohorts, one with a 49% loss to follow-up; the cross-sectional pools rest on four studies. It may be cited for the direction and rough size of the symptom association (low strength), for the list of what the cohorts could and could not show about lung function, and for the exposure limits; not for a size of effect adjusted for tobacco, for heavy long-term lung-function loss or for a causal effect.

key_findings.finding: 22 studies were included (10 prospective cohort, 12 cross-sectional) of 73 candidate articles; 3 were rated high risk of bias. 13 distinct outcomes were found and 5 could be pooled. Participants were older than 12 years with at least 30 days of lifetime cannabis use; English only; five databases from 1 January 1973 to 30 April 2018.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Selection; Results › Literature Search; Results › Study Characteristics

key_findings.finding: Exposure was low in most studies: across all outcomes and studies 1255 participants had more than 10 joint-years of exposure and 756 people who smoked cannabis only had more than 20 joint-years; across all prospective lung-function evaluations 243 people (131 cannabis-only) had more than 20 joint-years (1 joint a day for 20 years = 7300 joints, the authors' arithmetic). Methods of quantifying use varied (monthly, weekly or daily use; joint-years; cigarette-years).
key_findings.note: The two counts have different scopes (all studies and outcomes against prospective lung-function evaluations only) and should not be mixed.

key_findings.finding: Prospective cohorts, 2 studies pooled (Dunedin cohort, n = 1037, mean follow-up 15 years, use about once a week for a year on average; Los Angeles cohort, 299 people, mean 3.0 joints a day for 9.8 years, 49% lost to follow-up), people who used cannabis against people who did not: cough RR 2.04 (95% CI 1.02 to 4.06), RD 0.07 (0.02 to 0.13); sputum production RR 3.84 (1.62 to 9.07), RD 0.12 (-0.02 to 0.25); heterogeneity low. After the Knapp-Hartung adjustment the pooled RRs were not significant (cough P = 0.10; sputum P = 0.20). Both studies found that stopping cannabis was followed by a significant fall in respiratory symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend
key_findings.note: The abstract reports the unadjusted-looking intervals as showing increased risk. The legend's P values come from the small-sample method the Methods say was used.

key_findings.finding: Single prospective studies not pooled: the Tucson random-sample cohort (n = 1802, four surveys 1981 to 1988, moderate risk of bias) found current cannabis smoking associated with chronic cough OR 1.73 (1.21 to 2.47), chronic sputum OR 1.53 (1.08 to 2.18) and wheezing OR 2.01 (1.50 to 2.70); the Dunedin study found wheezing OR 1.55 (1.23 to 1.94), P < 0.001, and a trend for dyspnea OR 1.23 (0.97 to 1.56), P = 0.086.

Cross-sectional studies, 4 pooled (1 low and 3 moderate risk of bias; all included moderate to heavy use), people who used cannabis against people who did not: cough RR 4.37 (1.71 to 11.19), RD 0.18 (0.15 to 0.21); sputum production RR 3.40 (1.99 to 5.79), RD 0.14 (0.10 to 0.17); wheezing RR 2.83 (1.89 to 4.23), RD 0.22 (0.14 to 0.29); dyspnea RR 1.56 (1.33 to 1.83), RD 0.06 (-0.01 to 0.13). Knapp-Hartung P: cough 0.05, sputum 0.05, wheezing 0.01, dyspnea below 0.01. Heterogeneity was high for wheezing and is attributed to non-uniform exposure and symptom definitions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory Symptoms, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 legend; Table (wheezing comment); Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Chronic bronchitis and COPD: the Los Angeles cohort (3.0 joints a day, mean 9.8 years, 49% lost) found more bronchitis episodes, OR 2.3 (1.2 to 4.4), P = 0.011. Three cross-sectional studies pooled: RR 2.28 (0.68 to 7.72), RD 0.06 (-0.04 to 0.16), not significant (Knapp-Hartung P = 0.31). SPIROMICS (n = 1174, people currently or formerly smoking tobacco only): current use OR 0.87 (0.59 to 1.31), former use OR 1.0 (0.79 to 1.26). A high-risk-of-bias study found COPD prevalence higher by 0.3% (0.0% to 0.5%) per joint-year, with people who used cannabis and tobacco combined.
key_findings.locator: Results › Obstructive Lung Disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: FEV1: CARDIA (low risk of bias; 5115 adults aged 18 to 30 at the start; exposure minimal, 2 to 3 episodes a month): current use not associated with FEV1, adjusted mean difference -18 mL (-42 to 6.1), P = 0.32. A Los Angeles cohort (mean age 33, over 3.5 joints a day, 8 years): no significant fall in FEV1 in people who smoked cannabis continuously or intermittently against people who did not smoke it. Dunedin (10 years): no change. Tucson (4 to 5 cannabis cigarettes a week, moderate risk of bias): significant FEV1 reductions after 1 year (P < 0.01). Six cross-sectional studies: NHANES and SPIROMICS reported FEV1 only for cannabis and tobacco smoking combined; the other four found no effect but were small and young.
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in Pulmonary Function › FEV1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: FVC: CARDIA current use (more than 20 episodes in the past 30 days) +20 mL (-5.2 to 49), P = 0.03; lifetime use over 10 joint-years +59 mL (12 to 107), P = 0.01; Dunedin cannabis dependence +17.5 mL (-2.5 to 37.4), P = 0.087. Cross-sectional: SPIROMICS higher FVC in current and former use (P < 0.001); NHANES (mean 15.8 joint-years) +0.07% (SD 0.02%) per joint-year, P = 0.004; two studies found no effect (one at mean 50.4 joint-years, SD 4.6; one small, n = 50, high risk of bias).
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in Pulmonary Function › FVC, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The CARDIA current-use interval includes zero while P = 0.03.

key_findings.finding: FEV1-FVC ratio: Dunedin, 10 years, adjusted mean difference -0.19 (-0.42% to 0.04%), P = 0.100 (cumulative exposure not reported); Tucson significant reduction after 1 year. Cross-sectional: NHANES 2007 to 2010 (low risk of bias) over 20 joint-years against people who did not smoke cannabis, ratio below 70%: OR 2.1 (1.1 to 3.9), P = 0.02 after tobacco adjustment; the earlier NHANES study (moderate) no definite relationship; SPIROMICS (mean 30.1 joint-years, all with a tobacco-smoking history) positive association, P < 0.001; a Wellington study (n = 339, mean 54.2 joint-years, SD 75.3) marginally lower ratio, -1.1% (-2.6% to 0.1%); two further studies are described as showing no association (see reporting issues for one of them).
key_findings.locator: Results › Change in Pulmonary Function › FEV1-FVC Ratio, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Airway resistance and specific conductance of airways: all four studies (1 prospective, low risk of bias; 3 cross-sectional) reported higher resistance and lower conductance in people who smoked cannabis. Other respiratory outcomes: one prospective study found more outpatient visits for respiratory illness (colds, flu, sore throat) but no increase in hospital admission; a high-risk study found more respiratory problems; two cross-sectional studies found no difference in airway reactivity to methacholine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Airway Resistance and Specific Conductance of Airways; Results › Other Respiratory Outcomes

key_findings.finding: Strength of evidence (AHRQ method): low for cough, sputum production, wheezing and airway resistance; insufficient for dyspnea, obstructive lung disease, FEV1, FVC, FEV1-FVC ratio and other respiratory outcomes.

The authors say the lung-function evidence is limited by low exposure and young cohorts: tobacco's effect on FEV1 becomes measurable only after about 5 to 10 pack-years; obstructive lung disease develops in about a third of people who smoke tobacco long term and is usually identified after age 35 to 40; large cohorts of middle-aged to older people with heavier cannabis exposure may be needed. They add, as a conjecture, that few people may use enough cannabis to change lung function, so lung function may not be among its most important long-term health outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the Knapp-Hartung small-sample adjustment was applied, and the Figure 2 legend says the pooled prospective ratios were not significant after it (cough P = 0.10; sputum P = 0.20), yet the abstract and Results report intervals that exclude 1 (cough 1.02 to 4.06; sputum 1.62 to 9.07) as showing an increased risk.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two-study prospective pools are weaker than the abstract suggests; cite the ratios with the adjusted P values or lean on the cross-sectional pools and the single-cohort results.

reporting_issues.issue: CARDIA current-use FVC difference is given as 20 mL (-5.2 to 49 mL) with P = 0.03; the interval includes zero. Checked against the primary CARDIA paper (card sc_pletcher_2012): the 20 mL (-5.2 to 49) contrast is the heaviest current category (over 20 episodes in the past 30 days) and 0.030 is the P value for trend across all four current-intensity categories, not for that contrast; likewise P = 0.32 for the FEV1 difference of -18 mL (-42 to 6.1) is the trend P, and P = 0.01 for lifetime exposure over 10 joint-years is the trend P (0.013) across lifetime categories.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review attaches trend P values to single-category contrasts. Cite the CARDIA contrasts from the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The review describes the CARDIA FEV1 result (-18 mL, current use) as having minimal exposure, 2 to 3 episodes a month. In the primary paper 2 to 3 episodes a month is the median among people who smoked cannabis, while -18 mL is the contrast for over 20 episodes in 30 days (484 observations). The review also does not report the primary paper's spline result for current use (FEV1 slope -3.2 mL per episode a month at 20 episodes a month, 95% CI -5.8 to -0.6).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's 'no association' for CARDIA FEV1 understates the range of exposure the CARDIA contrast covers and omits a significant negative slope; the insufficient-evidence rating for lung function is unaffected, but the exposure wording should not be repeated.

reporting_issues.issue: In the cross-sectional pools the ratio and difference scales disagree: dyspnea RR 1.56 (1.33 to 1.83) has a confidence interval excluding 1 while RD 0.06 (-0.01 to 0.13) includes 0, and cough has a very narrow RD interval (0.15 to 0.21) beside a wide RR interval (1.71 to 11.19).
reporting_issues.consequence: Ratios and differences were pooled with different weights, so the absolute differences mostly reflect one or two large studies; the absolute figures should not be read as typical.

reporting_issues.issue: The text pools cross-sectional studies 'with low or moderate' risk of bias from a set of 7 (3 low, 3 moderate, 1 high), but the abstract and Table show 4 pooled studies (1 low and 3 moderate); two low-risk studies are not accounted for in the text, and the identity of the four is only in the forest-plot image.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which studies make up the cross-sectional pools could not be checked from the text; Figure 3 values were not extracted.

reporting_issues.issue: In the FEV1-FVC section the two remaining cross-sectional studies (refs 20 and 21) are said to show no association with a reduced ratio, but the next sentences say the study of ref 20 (38 people who used cannabis only) found significantly lower ratios (P < 0.05) in men who currently smoked cannabis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text contradicts itself about one small study; the FEV1-FVC evidence is rated insufficient in any case.

reporting_issues.issue: The FEV1 row of the Table refers to 'the experimental study' limited by lack of adjustment for key confounders, but the Results describe no experimental study for FEV1 (4 prospective and 6 cross-sectional studies only).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor text-to-table mismatch; the FEV1 conclusion rests on the studies listed in the Results.

reporting_issues.issue: Two different counts of heavy exposure appear: Results give 756 people who smoked cannabis only with more than 20 joint-years across all outcomes and studies; the Discussion gives 243 people (131 cannabis-only) across prospective lung-function evaluations.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not an error, but the scopes differ; a citation of 'few heavy smokers' must name the 243 (131) figure for lung function.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction says cannabis smoke may contain particulate matter, toxic gases and aromatic hydrocarbons at 20 times the concentration of tobacco smoke, citing a 1975 book chapter; no included study tests this.
reporting_issues.consequence: Background framing only; it should not be cited as a finding of the review.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6231497 (author manuscript; abstract, introduction, methods, results, strength-of-evidence table as text, discussion, funding and disclosures read; Figures 1 to 3, including the flow chart and all forest plots, are images and their values were not extracted; the Supplement PDF was not opened)
